claims.text: Premelting onset in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is governed by preferential early mobility of Fe and Cu.
Element-specific local energetic environments drive the preferential early mobility of Fe and Cu.
Preferential Fe and Cu mobility initiates a two-phase melting transition rather than a persistent liquid shell.
The melting temperature increases toward the bulk limit as nanoparticle radius increases, following an inverse-radius dependence.
The initial nanoparticles have a random equiatomic FCC Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu lattice with a lattice parameter of 3.52 Å.
The simulations compare nanoparticles with radii of approximately 5–40 Å under a controlled heating ramp.
Heating proceeds from 300 K to 2500 K in 20 K increments, with 100 ps equilibration and 100 ps averaging at each increment.
Fe has a potential energy about 0.5 eV higher than the other species.
Cu has a comparatively low melting point that contributes to its early diffusion.
Early diffusion begins in approximately the outer two to three atomic layers and then propagates into the core.
Melting proceeds through competition between solid and liquid phases.
The transition lacks a persistent liquid layer and instead exhibits gradual, core-propagating enhanced mobility.
The fitted bulk melting limit is approximately 2184 K.
Fe and Cu develop increased mean-square displacements at lower temperatures than Ni, Cr, and Co.
The overall random equiatomic elemental distribution remains largely unclustered during the predicted early-mobility regime.
For particles near a radius of 5 Å, preferential Fe and Cu mobility may be negligible.
Changing the interatomic potential or considering sizes outside approximately 5–40 Å may produce deviations from the predicted behavior.

contradictions.description: A controlled temperature ramp and repeated velocity rescaling alter particle energy and therefore are not strictly compatible with an NVE ensemble, which conserves total energy.

The boundary explicitly allows preferential Fe and Cu mobility to be negligible near R ≈ 5 Å, whereas the falsification rule can be read as treating failure to observe that preferential mobility anywhere in the tested 5–40 Å range as decisive falsification.
